THE LABOR CODE SECTION 1102.6 BURDEN FRAMEWORK FOR WHISTLEBLOWER-RETALIATION DISCHARGE CLAIMS (LAB. CODE §§ 1102.5, 1102.6, 1105; LAWSON V. PPG ARCHITECTURAL FINISHES; VATALARO V. COUNTY OF SACRAMENTO; VERVERKA V. DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS; CACI NOS. 4603, 4604) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

THE SECTION 1102.6 BURDEN FRAMEWORK — APPLICABILITY NOTE
This information sheet concerns Jordan Lee’s former position as Territory Manager with Acme, Inc., recorded here as having ended on August 28, 2026; the concern Jordan Lee is recorded here as having raised or refused to take part in, described as: a report to the company ethics hotline about mislabeled product; and Acme, Inc.’s stated reason for the separation, recorded here as: failure to meet a performance improvement plan. It describes what Labor Code sections 1102.5, 1102.6, and 1105, the California Supreme Court’s decision in Lawson v. PPG Architectural Finishes, Inc. (2022), the Court of Appeal’s decisions in Vatalaro v. County of Sacramento (2022) and Ververka v. Department of Veterans Affairs (2024), and the Judicial Council’s civil jury instructions say about how a whistleblower-retaliation claim under section 1102.5 is presented and decided: the two-step framework the Legislature wrote into section 1102.6, the employee’s preponderance showing that protected activity was a “contributing factor” in the adverse action, the holding that the three-step McDonnell Douglas test does not govern these claims, the employer’s burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that it would have acted for legitimate, independent reasons anyway, how the framework operates on summary judgment, the reported holding that a successful same-decision showing bars relief entirely under this statute, and the jury instructions that carry the framework to trial. Whether Jordan Lee engaged in activity that section 1102.5 protects, whether any such activity contributed to Acme, Inc.’s decision, whether Acme, Inc. could carry the second-step burden, and what relief (if any) would follow are facts this sheet does not determine. Naming the parties, the date, the concern, and the stated reason here does not itself establish that any rule described below applies to their separation, and this sheet states what the statutes, the courts, and the instructions say rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular claim or defense.

THE STATUTE ITSELF: SECTION 1102.6’S TWO-STEP FRAMEWORK
Labor Code section 1102.6, added in 2003, states a single sentence that assigns both sides a burden in a section 1102.5 whistleblower case. Step one belongs to the employee: it must be demonstrated by a preponderance of the evidence that an activity section 1102.5 protects was “a contributing factor” in the alleged prohibited action. Step two then belongs to the employer: it has the burden of proof to demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that the alleged action would have occurred for legitimate, independent reasons even if the employee had not engaged in protected activity. In Lawson v. PPG Architectural Finishes, Inc. (2022), the California Supreme Court described that sentence as supplying the substantive standards and burdens of proof for both parties, and as a complete set of instructions for the presentation and evaluation of evidence rather than the codification of an affirmative defense alone. The statute applies by its terms in “a civil action or administrative proceeding brought pursuant to Section 1102.5,” and Labor Code section 1105 preserves the injured employee’s action for damages for a violation of the chapter that contains section 1102.5. Whether the framework applies to Jordan Lee’s separation from Acme, Inc., and how either step would come out, are facts this clause does not determine.

WHAT ACTIVITY SECTION 1102.5 PROTECTS, AND THEREFORE WHAT STEP ONE IS ABOUT
Section 1102.6 allocates burdens only for a claim “brought pursuant to Section 1102.5,” so the activity that step one asks about is the activity section 1102.5 protects. Subdivision (b) bars retaliation for disclosing information — or because the employer believes the employee disclosed or may disclose information — to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee, to another employee with authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance, or by providing information to or testifying before a public body conducting an investigation, hearing, or inquiry, where the employee has reasonable cause to believe the information discloses a violation of a state or federal statute or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation, and it says so regardless of whether disclosing the information is part of the employee’s job duties. Subdivision (c) bars retaliation for refusing to participate in an activity that would result in such a violation or noncompliance, and subdivision (d) extends protection to rights exercised in a former employment. Lawson summarized the statute as providing whistleblower protections to employees who disclose wrongdoing to authorities. Whether a report to the company ethics hotline about mislabeled product, as Jordan Lee raised it, falls within any of these subdivisions is a fact this clause does not determine.

STEP ONE: WHAT “CONTRIBUTING FACTOR” MEANS, AND WHY PRETEXT IS NOT PART OF IT
Step one asks whether protected activity was “a contributing factor” in the adverse action, proved by a preponderance of the evidence. Lawson explained that this standard lets a plaintiff satisfy the statutory burden even when other, legitimate factors also contributed to the decision, and that a plaintiff therefore does not have to show that the employer’s nonretaliatory reason was pretextual: even if the employer had a genuine, nonretaliatory reason, the plaintiff still carries the assigned burden if the employer also had at least one retaliatory reason that contributed to the action. The Court added that the three-part McDonnell Douglas test was not written to evaluate claims involving multiple reasons for the challenged action. The Judicial Council’s instruction CACI No. 4603 states the standard for juries in the same terms, defining a contributing factor as any factor that, alone or in connection with other factors, tends to affect the outcome of a decision, and adding that a contributing factor can be proved even when other legitimate factors also contributed. Whether protected activity contributed at all to Acme, Inc.’s decision about Jordan Lee is a fact this clause does not determine.

LAWSON’S HOLDING: MCDONNELL DOUGLAS DOES NOT GOVERN A SECTION 1102.5 CLAIM
Before Lawson, California courts were split. When section 1102.5 was enacted in 1984 it carried no procedural provision, so courts borrowed the three-step burden-shifting test of McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green (1973) 411 U.S. 792 — prima facie case, a legitimate reason articulated by the employer, then pretext. After section 1102.6 took effect in 2004 some courts applied the statute while others continued to apply McDonnell Douglas without mentioning it. The California Supreme Court answered a question certified by the Ninth Circuit and clarified that section 1102.6, and not McDonnell Douglas, supplies the applicable framework for litigating and adjudicating section 1102.5 whistleblower claims, and that employees need not satisfy the McDonnell Douglas test to make out a case of unlawful retaliation. The Court disapproved three Court of Appeal decisions — Hager v. County of Los Angeles, Mokler v. County of Orange, and Patten v. Grant Joint Union High School District — to the extent they were inconsistent with the opinion. Which framework a court would apply to any claim Jordan Lee might assert against Acme, Inc., and how it would come out, are matters this clause does not determine.

STEP TWO: THE EMPLOYER’S CLEAR-AND-CONVINCING SHOWING OF LEGITIMATE, INDEPENDENT REASONS
If the employee carries step one, section 1102.6 gives the employer the burden of proof — not merely a burden of producing evidence of some legitimate reason — and sets the standard at clear and convincing evidence. Vatalaro v. County of Sacramento (2022) identified three ways the old three-part test misstated that obligation: it understated the standard, which section 1102.6 sets above a preponderance; it understated the showing, because merely having one legitimate reason is not enough where illegitimate reasons principally motivated the decision; and it wrongly required the employee to prove pretext. Under the statute the employer must show that the alleged action would have occurred for legitimate, independent reasons even if the employee had not engaged in protected activity. The Judicial Council states the same rule as an affirmative defense in CACI No. 4604 and describes the setting as a mixed-motive case in which there is evidence of both a retaliatory and a legitimate reason. Whether Acme, Inc. could make that showing as to failure to meet a performance improvement plan is a fact this clause does not determine.

THE SAME FRAMEWORK APPLIES ON SUMMARY JUDGMENT
The employer in Lawson argued that even if section 1102.6 governs at trial, McDonnell Douglas should still govern at summary judgment. The California Supreme Court rejected that split: nothing in the text of section 1102.6 supports a bifurcated approach under which one standard governs on summary judgment and another at trial. The Court reasoned that a bifurcated rule would require plaintiffs to show at summary judgment that retaliation was, in effect, the only factor, that the purpose of summary judgment is not to weed out cases that might prove meritorious at trial, and that the parties’ burdens at summary judgment generally depend on their burdens at trial. The Court also said that an employer is not barred from raising a same-decision defense on summary judgment. Vatalaro applied that approach, affirming summary judgment for the employer on the ground that it had supplied sufficient evidence to satisfy the more demanding section 1102.6 standard even though it had argued the wrong test below. How any motion in a case involving Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. would be decided is a fact this clause does not determine.

Naming the parties, the date, the concern, and the stated reason here does not itself establish that any rule described below applies to their separation, and this sheet states what the statutes, the courts, and the instructions say rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular claim or defense.

Labor Code section 1102.6, added in 2003, states a single sentence that assigns both sides a burden in a section 1102.5 whistleblower case. Step one belongs to the employee: it must be demonstrated by a preponderance of the evidence that an activity section 1102.5 protects was “a contributing factor” in the alleged prohibited action. Step two then belongs to the employer: it has the burden of proof to demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that the alleged action would have occurred for legitimate, independent reasons even if the employee had not engaged in protected activity. In Lawson v. PPG Architectural Finishes, Inc. (2022), the California Supreme Court described that sentence as supplying the substantive standards and burdens of proof for both parties, and as a complete set of instructions for the presentation and evaluation of evidence rather than the codification of an affirmative defense alone. The statute applies by its terms in “a civil action or administrative proceeding brought pursuant to Section 1102.5,” and Labor Code section 1105 preserves the injured employee’s action for damages for a violation of the chapter that contains section 1102.5. Whether the framework applies to Jordan Lee’s separation from Acme, Inc., and how either step would come out, are facts this clause does not determine.

Lawson explained that this standard lets a plaintiff satisfy the statutory burden even when other, legitimate factors also contributed to the decision, and that a plaintiff therefore does not have to show that the employer’s nonretaliatory reason was pretextual: even if the employer had a genuine, nonretaliatory reason, the plaintiff still carries the assigned burden if the employer also had at least one retaliatory reason that contributed to the action. expectedJSON.body: Before Lawson, California courts were split. When section 1102.5 was enacted in 1984 it carried no procedural provision, so courts borrowed the three-step burden-shifting test of McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green (1973) 411 U.S. 792 — prima facie case, a legitimate reason articulated by the employer, then pretext. After section 1102.6 took effect in 2004 some courts applied the statute while others continued to apply McDonnell Douglas without mentioning it. The Court disapproved three Court of Appeal decisions — Hager v. County of Los Angeles, Mokler v. County of Orange, and Patten v. Grant Joint Union High School District — to the extent they were inconsistent with the opinion. Which framework a court would apply to any claim Jordan Lee might assert against Acme, Inc., and how it would come out, are matters this clause does not determine.

Vatalaro is a Court of Appeal decision from the Third Appellate District and Ververka is from the First District, Division One; neither binds the other Courts of Appeal, and the California Supreme Court has not addressed the questions they decide beyond Lawson itself. expectedJSON.body: The employer in Lawson argued that even if section 1102.6 governs at trial, McDonnell Douglas should still govern at summary judgment. The California Supreme Court rejected that split: nothing in the text of section 1102.6 supports a bifurcated approach under which one standard governs on summary judgment and another at trial. The Court reasoned that a bifurcated rule would require plaintiffs to show at summary judgment that retaliation was, in effect, the only factor, that the purpose of summary judgment is not to weed out cases that might prove meritorious at trial, and that the parties’ burdens at summary judgment generally depend on their burdens at trial. The Court also said that an employer is not barred from raising a same-decision defense on summary judgment. Vatalaro applied that approach, affirming summary judgment for the employer on the ground that it had supplied sufficient evidence to satisfy the more demanding section 1102.6 standard even though it had argued the wrong test below. How any motion in a case involving Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. would be decided is a fact this clause does not determine.

For that reason, the parties’ burdens of proof at summary judgment generally depend on their burdens of proof at trial.

expectedJSON.body: Under the Fair Employment and Housing Act, an employer’s same-decision showing limits remedies rather than defeating liability outright. In Ververka v. Department of Veterans Affairs (2024) the plaintiff argued that the same rule should follow under section 1102.6, so that a whistleblower who proved a contributing factor could still obtain declaratory relief and attorney’s fees after the employer carried step two. The Court of Appeal rejected that reading. It reasoned that section 1102.6 is a procedural statute the Legislature wrote for these claims, that it applies by its terms in a “civil action” without limitation and exempts no category of relief, and that a straightforward reading is that a plaintiff is barred from all relief once the employer satisfies its second-step burden. The court treated the presence of section 1102.6 as what distinguishes these claims from the FEHA analysis, where no comparable procedural statute existed. Whether any court would reach the same conclusion in a case involving Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc., and what relief would be available there, are matters this clause does not determine.

expectedJSON.body: Lawson did not treat section 1102.6 as unique. The Court noted that other courts facing burden-shifting frameworks similar to section 1102.6 had likewise found McDonnell Douglas inapplicable, pointing to First Amendment retaliation claims governed by Mt. Healthy City Board of Ed. v. Doyle (1977) 429 U.S. 274 — which assigns the plaintiff an initial burden on whether protected conduct was a substantial or motivating factor and then assigns the defendant the burden of showing it would have made the same decision anyway — and observing that nearly every federal circuit to consider applying McDonnell Douglas in that setting had thought the idea a poor one. The Court also pointed to the federal Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, enacted shortly before section 1102.6, which contains a nearly identical burden-shifting framework for whistleblower cases and which courts have generally read as displacing rather than supplementing McDonnell Douglas. How any of these federal frameworks would bear on a claim involving Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. is a matter this clause does not determine.
